articles.title: Postgres "deadlock detected": Fix the Lock Order First, Then Add a Retry
articles.excerpt: Postgres raises ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01) when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The durable fix is to make every code path lock rows in the same order; a retry on 40P…
articles.body: Postgres raises ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01 ) when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The durable fix is to make every code path lock rows in the same order; a retry on 40P01 is the safety net, not the cure. If you only add the retry, you hide the bug and pay for it in latency. What does the error actually say? This is the shape of the message you get in the application and the server log: ERROR: deadlock detected DETAIL: Process 8121 waits for ShareLock on transaction 90417; blocked by process 8130. Process 8130 waits for ShareLock on transaction 90416; blocked by process 8121. HINT: See server log for query details. CONTEXT: while updating tuple (0,12) in relation "accounts" Read it as a cycle.

articles.title: I finally get why people ask for an uncensored LLM API, and it’s not for the reason everyone assumes
articles.excerpt: A few months ago I watched a completely normal automation fail in the dumbest possible way. It wasn’t generating malware. It was summarizing a support thread, extracting the customer issue, and postin…
articles.body: A few months ago I watched a completely normal automation fail in the dumbest possible way. It wasn’t generating malware. It wasn’t writing abuse. It wasn’t doing anything remotely edgy. It was summarizing a support thread, extracting the customer issue, and posting the result to Slack. Then the model started acting weird. One run was fine. The next run sanitized half the answer. The run after that refused entirely because the ticket mentioned account abuse, credential resets, and suspicious login attempts. Same workflow. Same business context. Totally different behavior. That’s when this clicked for me: Most developers asking for an "uncensored LLM API" are not asking for chaos. They’re asking for a model that doesn’t panic in the middle of a harmless production job.

articles.excerpt: Tested on NetBox 4.5, FortiOS 7.4, RouterOS 7.23 (long-term) and Proxmox VE 8.3 I wanted NetBox to reflect what my lab actually runs, not what I remembered to type into it. So I wrote a script that re…
articles.body: Tested on NetBox 4.5, FortiOS 7.4, RouterOS 7.23 (long-term) and Proxmox VE 8.3 I wanted NetBox to reflect what my lab actually runs, not what I remembered to type into it. So I wrote a script that reads a FortiGate, a MikroTik and a Proxmox host every night and reconciles NetBox with what they report. Writing the collectors took an afternoon. The hard part was a different question: this thing runs unattended, every day, with write access to my source of truth. What must it never do? I ended up with four rules. Each one I either tested on purpose or learned by watching it fail.

articles.title: A publishing gate for 53,000 server-rendered pages
articles.excerpt: The problem with static builds When a site has about 53,000 possible pages and a business profile edit can change any of them, rebuilding a static site is not practical. Each edit would require regene…
articles.body: The problem with static builds When a site has about 53,000 possible pages and a business profile edit can change any of them, rebuilding a static site is not practical. Each edit would require regenerating a large portion of the site, and the delay between an edit and the updated page would depend on build time. Server rendering on Workers and D1 The site runs Astro 5 with server rendering on Cloudflare Workers, using a D1 database for storage. Each request reaches a Worker that queries D1 for the current data and renders the HTML. Because rendering happens on demand, an edit to a profile is visible on the next request without a build step. The pages table as a publishing gate Not every record in the database is ready to be public. A separate pages table acts as a publishing gate.

articles.body: Si mantienes un programa de facturación en España, ya sabes que llega VERI*FACTU , el sistema de la Agencia Tributaria que desarrolla el Real Decreto 1007/2023 (la «ley antifraude»). Cada factura tiene que generar un registro de facturación con una huella encadenada a la anterior. Ese registro se envía a la AEAT y la factura impresa lleva un código QR que el cliente puede verificar. La AEAT publica la especificación en varios PDF y XSD. En PHP y .NET ya hay librerías asentadas, pero en Python no había ninguna completa, así que la he escrito y la he publicado como open source: verifactu-python ( pip install verifactu-sdk ). En este artículo veremos las cuatro piezas del sistema y cómo resolver cada una. 1. La huella (hash) encadenada Es la parte en la que más gente se equivoca.

articles.title: I checked nine free RFC 3161 endpoints against the EU Trusted List. None is qualified. Five of the companies are.
articles.excerpt: On 16 October 2026 I sent one timestamp request to each of nine public, free RFC 3161 endpoints and looked up the certificate that signed each reply in the EU Trusted List. All nine answered. All nine…
articles.body: On 16 October 2026 I sent one timestamp request to each of nine public, free RFC 3161 endpoints and looked up the certificate that signed each reply in the EU Trusted List. All nine answered. All nine tokens verified (message imprint and nonce echoed back correctly). None of the nine is a qualified timestamp under eIDAS. The list I checked against: LOTL sequence 397, issued 2026-10-15, 29 member-state lists downloaded and signature-verified, 1,443 TSA/QTST entries of which 915 are granted today. Snapshot SHA-256 d1700e6a…c85d , LOTL SHA-256 a36d0053…70e6 . Hungary and Portugal didn't download (TLS cut the connection), so a Hungarian or Portuguese endpoint would have come back "not checked", not "not qualified". None of the nine is in either country.

articles.body: The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station wish that we could all see Earth as they just did. An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA. "You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere , and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission .

articles.body: I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective. The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet , which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside.

articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES weather satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite! GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite . GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1. The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space.
